challenges.title: The list that changed twice

questions.prompt: What do the two println calls output, in order?
options: [A, B] then [A, C]
[A] then [A, C]
[A, B, C] then [A, B, C]
[A, B] then [A, B, C]
questions.explanation: alias and original reference the same list. copy is a new list containing the original elements at the time of construction. Adding B changes original; adding C changes only copy.

challenges.title: Follow the return value

options: Line 6 returns immediately; output is 2
Line 8 changes the returned value; output is 3 3
Line 6 captures 2, finally prints 3, then main prints 2
finally runs before try; output is 3 2
questions.explanation: The return expression is evaluated at line 6, capturing the primitive value 2. The finally block then executes and prints 3 plus a space. Changing the local variable does not change the already captured return value. Output: 3 2.

challenges.title: A cache that forgets its keys

questions.prompt: In this example the lookup returns null. What is the root cause and reliable fix?
options: HashMap compares only identity; use TreeMap
The hash changes after insertion; make equality/hash fields immutable
get deletes expired values; use containsKey
The map is too small; increase initial capacity
questions.explanation: HashMap stores the insertion hash. Changing id changes hashCode and makes the lookup hash differ from the stored hash, even for the same object. Use immutable key identity (for example, a final id) or remove the key before mutation and reinsert it.

challenges.title: Catch the missing last item

questions.prompt: Which smallest test fails now and passes when the loop uses i < prices.length?
options: total(new int[]{}) == 0
total(new int[]{0}) == 0
total(new int[]{7}) == 7
total(new int[]{0, 0}) == 0
questions.explanation: A singleton nonzero array isolates the skipped final element. The buggy loop never runs and returns 0 rather than 7. Empty arrays and zero-only inputs mask the defect.

challenges.title: The AI patch that loses updates

questions.prompt: Two threads call record("/api") concurrently. What did the AI patch miss?
options: ConcurrentHashMap is never thread-safe
The read-modify-write is not atomic; use counts.merge(route, 1, Integer::sum)
Integer must be replaced by int
getOrDefault always returns zero for concurrent maps
questions.explanation: Individual map operations are safe, but two threads can read the same previous count and both write the same incremented count. merge performs the update atomically for this key. A concurrent collection alone does not make a multi-step algorithm atomic.

practiceCase.title: The missing requests
practiceCase.summary: The request log says 10,000 requests completed. The traffic report counts fewer. A confident AI proposal claims to fix the race. Investigate before accepting it.
requirements: Count every completed handler invocation once, including handlers that throw.
Keep counts independent for each route, with concurrent calls allowed.
Read a report only after the relevant handlers have completed.
Prefer per-key coordination; do not serialize unrelated routes without explaining the tradeoff.
assumptions: Java 17+; a framework-neutral service excerpt, not a complete HTTP application.
One shared RequestCounter instance is injected into both services.
Routes are canonical non-null strings; counts remain within the integer range.
Incident observations are authored practice fixtures, not a live load test.

proposal.label: Seeded AI proposal
proposal.disclosure: An authored practice proposal, not a live model response. Assess its claim against the case.
proposal.claim: Use compare-and-replace so concurrent requests cannot overwrite each other. One conditional replacement is enough; no retry is necessary.

hints: Trace the finally block into the shared counter, then follow the reporting read path. A failed handler still reaches finally.
Try making both requests read the same old count before either writes. A concurrent map does not make the whole sequence atomic.
A conditional replace can return false. If that result is ignored, which completed request contributed no increment? An atomic merge is one repair.

reference.explanation: Both requests can read 0 and then each write 1. The map safely performs each individual operation, but the read-modify-write sequence is not atomic. The proposed compare-and-replace still loses an increment when one replacement fails and its false return is ignored.
reference.flow: RequestController.handle runs the handler, then finally records completion even on an exception. RequestCounter owns the shared per-route map. TrafficReportService reads that same counter after completion and returns an immutable TrafficReport.
reference.fix: Use ConcurrentHashMap.merge for the per-route increment. A correctly retried compare-and-replace loop or a lock covering the entire read/write can also be correct; discuss contention and ownership.
reference.test: Force both workers to observe the initial value before either write. The required final count is 2. The original method and seeded proposal both yield 1 under this schedule. The reference merge yields 2. Also preserve failed-handler counting and route isolation.
review: Does the explanation connect completion, shared state, and reporting across files, including the exception path?
Does the reasoning show a legal interleaving rather than merely naming concurrency?
Does the critique identify the ignored false result of replace and verify the proposal instead of trusting its confidence?
Does the written patch actually implement an atomic per-route update and explain tradeoffs? This needs review; it is not parsed or run.
Does the proposed test control overlap, assert 2, preserve error-path counting, and isolate routes? Written test code is not run.
